questions.q: How do you create a variable in PowerShell?
options: $name = value — no separate declaration step, and no type is required up front
You must run New-Variable and specify a type before assigning any value
Variables can only be created inside a .ps1 script file, never interactively
Every variable must be declared with the [var] keyword
questions.explain: PowerShell variables start with a dollar sign and are created the moment you assign them a value.

options: PowerShell infers type from the value — quotes make "5" a string, so + becomes text concatenation instead of addition
PowerShell always treats + as addition regardless of quotes
This is a bug in PowerShell with no real explanation
"5" and 5 are always treated identically in PowerShell
questions.explain: PowerShell's dynamic typing means the quoted "5" is a string, so + concatenates instead of adding.

questions.q: Which of these forces a variable to a specific type explicitly?
options: [int]$retryCount = 3
$retryCount == int(3)
retryCount: int = 3
PowerShell has no way to force an explicit type
questions.explain: Putting the type name in brackets before the variable, like [int]$retryCount = 3, forces that type explicitly.

questions.q: What does piping a variable into Get-Member show you?
options: The object's real type name plus every property and method available on it
Only the variable's current value, nothing else
A list of every variable currently defined in the session
Whether the variable was created in the console or in VS Code
questions.explain: Get-Member's output starts with the real TypeName and lists all properties and methods on that object.
